entities.name: Demophilus of Thespiae
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Demophilus, son of Diadromes, commanded the contingent of 700 Thespian hoplites who stood alongside the 300 Spartans under King Leonidas I at the Battle of Thermopylae in 480 BCE. This Hellenic commander from the Boeotian city-state of Thespiae epitomized the fierce, if ultimately doomed, resistance of a coalition of Greek city-states against the colossal invading forces of the Achaemenid Persian Empire. His actions, recorded primarily by Herodotus in his *Histories*, cemented Thespiae's place in the collective memory of Greek heroism and sacrifice during the Greco-Persian Wars, a conflict that profoundly shaped the geopolitical landscape of the ancient Mediterranean and the trajectory of Western civilization. The Thespians, unlike many other Greek forces, chose to remain and fight to the death, making Demophilus a symbol of unwavering resolve in the face of overwhelming odds.

In the summer of 480 BCE, as Xerxes I's massive Persian army advanced through northern Greece, Demophilus led his 700 Thespian soldiers to the narrow pass of Thermopylae. There, they joined the defensive force spearheaded by King Leonidas I of Sparta, aiming to block the Persian advance and allow time for the rest of Greece to mobilize. For three days, the small Greek contingent, positioned strategically, repelled successive waves of Persian attacks, inflicting heavy casualties. When the treachery of Ephialtes revealed a mountain path allowing the Persians to outflank the defenders, Leonidas ordered the majority of the Greek forces to retreat. However, Demophilus and his 700 Thespians, along with the 300 Spartans and a few hundred Thebans, chose to remain, fully aware of their impending doom. They made their final stand on the "hill of the last stand," fighting to the last man, including Demophilus himself, who perished in the brutal engagement.
